This study presents a method for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth ($\tau_{\rm A}$) in the 530 nm band using wide-field photometry, eliminating the need for absolute calibration. By combining this method with simultaneous measurements from a sun photometer, we derived a calibration constant for the photometer. The resulting calibration constant aligns closely with the value obtained through standard calibration procedures. Furthermore, the proposed method offers a rapid means to detect sudden shifts in atmospheric conditions, such as the passage of clouds or dust. The data collection system is fully automated and requires minimal human intervention. The analysis was conducted on 100 days of observations recorded in Mexico City between 2015 and 2017. These observations were compared with measurements from a sun photometer and a lidar, yielding a root mean square error of 0.03. The data were also utilized to generate a 24-hour aerosol optical depth map, which was validated against satellite imagery from the MODIS instrument. The interaction between two heavy quarks at short distances is governed by the QCD potential, which can be expressed as a perturbative series involving powers of the quark separation. At large distances, this interaction is characterized by confinement, leading to the formation of heavy quark-antiquark pairs into mesons or trios into baryons. This review examines the theoretical framework for both the perturbative and confining components of the potential, with a specific focus on the static potential and its applications to quarkonium. It also covers the Nambu--Beckon string model, the AdS/CFT correspondence, and the concept of quarkonium suppression in quark--gluon plasmas. Finally, the discussion extends to the in-medium potential and its behavior within the context of quarkonium dissociation. Our analysis indicates that the AdS/CFT model aligns well with lattice QCD results for the static potential at large separations, whereas the Nambu--Beckon model underestimates the potential strength in this regime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the in-medium potential derived from AdS/CFT exhibits dissociation patterns consistent with lattice QCD findings. Additionally, we observe that the in-medium potential predicted by AdS/CFT shows qualitative agreement with the dissociation behavior observed in the perturbative potential. These results suggest that the AdS/CFT model could serve as a viable approximation for the in-medium potential of quarkonia. Nevertheless, it is important to acknowledge that this model relies on assumptions that may not hold under all physical conditions. Our findings also imply that the in-medium potential for quarkonia is likely weaker than the vacuum potential at large distances. This weakening could explain why the $2S$ state dissociates at temperatures lower than the $1S$ state, a phenomenon that aligns with lattice QCD data. Ultimately, the in-medium potential represents a crucial component for understanding quarkonium dissociation. We conclude by outlining future research directions. Furthermore, the iterative algorithm successfully achieves near-optimal fair-throughput and sum-throughput levels. The phenomenon of strangeness enhancement in high-multiplicity proton-proton (pp) collisions has been extensively documented, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This paper presents a detailed analysis of the ratio of kaon to pion yields, $R_{K/\pi} = Y_K/Y_\pi$, across a wide range of collision energies ($\sqrt{s}$) and multiplicities in both pp and heavy-ion (AA) collisions. We observe that in central AA collisions, $R_{K/\pi}$ exhibits a significant rise with increasing energy, whereas in pp collisions, the rise is much more gradual. Furthermore, we find that the $R_{K/\pi}$ yield in central AA collisions aligns with a power-law dependence on the total multiplicity of charged particles, $N_{\rm ch}$, with a slope of approximately 0.15. In contrast, the slope for pp collisions is significantly lower, around 0.03. These results indicate that the mechanisms driving strangeness enhancement in high-multiplicity pp and AA collisions are fundamentally distinct. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $R_{K/\pi}$ yield in central AA collisions can be accurately predicted by scaling the $R_{K/\pi}$ from the most central (20--30%) pp collisions by a factor of roughly 100, suggesting that the most central pp collisions serve as the fundamental building blocks for AA collisions. Finally, we show that the $R_{K/\pi}$ yield in pp collisions follows a universal power-law relationship with the energy of the most energetic particle, $E_{\rm hardest}$, a trend that also holds for AA collisions. These findings suggest that the enhancement of strangeness in high-multiplicity pp and AA collisions originates from the same fundamental mechanism: an increase in the number of parton-parton interactions. However, the specific mechanisms responsible for generating high $E_{\rm hardest}$ in central pp and AA collisions differ. These results imply that the most central pp collisions act as the building blocks for the most central AA collisions. Such conclusions carry significant implications for understanding the creation of quark-gluon plasma in both pp and AA collisions. We analyze a scenario where two agents sequentially choose between two tasks, each with a distinct difficulty level, to maximize their combined rewards. Furthermore, we introduce a contextual MAB algorithm that achieves a regret close to this lower bound. Our findings indicate that the optimal strategy involves assigning the easier task to the agent with the higher contextual value, while the harder task goes to the other. To validate our approach, we conduct experiments using both synthetic and real-world data, demonstrating the algorithm's effectiveness in practical applications. These results offer valuable insights for optimizing task allocation in multi-agent systems. Our work contributes to the fields of multi-agent systems, contextual multi-armed bandits, and regret analysis. We introduce a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme designed to simulate non-equilibrium quantum correlations beyond the limits of conventional linear response theory. The results indicate that, following a sudden expansion, the system's quantum correlations initially align with linear sound modes but eventually transition into non-equilibrium behaviors characterized by "quantum clumping." This phenomenon, which resembles classical vortex formation in gases, is captured by our linearized Monte Carlo method only when non-equilibrium effects remain weak. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this non-equilibrium behavior can be effectively modeled by extending the linearized model to include a simple anomalous diffusion term. Ultimately, we conclude that, for weak non-equilibrium scenarios, the evolution of quantum correlations can be accurately described by a generalized Fokker-Planck equation that incorporates anomalous diffusion. Such techniques could be valuable for analyzing recent heavy ion collision data. Additionally, the linearized Monte Carlo framework presented here can be readily adapted to simulate non-equilibrium quantum systems with complex interactions, such as those governed by non-Abelian gauge theories. Ultimately, this work provides a practical and efficient tool for investigating non-equilibrium dynamics in a wide range of quantum systems.

Finally, we provide the MOAD dataset and all associated code to the community to facilitate future research. This paper introduces a unified framework for unsupervised and supervised feature extraction that leverages the inherent connection between these tasks. The approach begins by training an unsupervised feature extractor, which is then refined through supervised fine-tuning using labeled data. We formulate this problem as a two-stage optimization task, employing a differentiable approximation of the unsupervised extraction process to enable end-to-end optimization. Extensive experiments across multiple domains demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction. Furthermore, the framework yields significant improvements in downstream classification tasks, including semantic segmentation and image captioning. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhenghuilong/UnifiedFeatureExtraction. Our key contributions are as follows: (1) We propose a unified framework for unsupervised and supervised feature extraction, achieving state-of-the-art results in both domains; (2) We develop a differentiable approximation of the unsupervised extraction process, enabling an end-to-end optimization strategy; (3) We validate the framework's effectiveness in various downstream tasks, such as semantic segmentation and image captioning.

This study introduces a novel, generalizable proof-based methodology to enhance the certified accuracy of PC models against T. Our approach, termed TPC (Transform-Point-Certify), integrates a twisting transformation into the certification pipeline. By applying a relaxation technique to the transformed PCs, we establish a tighter upper bound for certification, thereby improving certified accuracy. We validated this framework across various PC models and twisting angles, demonstrating significant gains. Specifically, under a 20-degree twist, our method improved certified accuracy by 13.7% compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, we extended the TPC framework to handle multiple twisting angles simultaneously, achieving higher accuracy levels for specific transformation ranges. The source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyixiang/Point-Cloud-Certification.

This environment leverages a specialized compiler that transforms C source code into a hybrid representation combining symbolic and concrete domains. This representation enables the execution of concrete inputs alongside the analysis of symbolic inputs, which are subsequently concretized to generate test cases. These cases are run against the original source code, and the resulting outputs are compared to detect failures. Upon failure, the system automatically generates a proof trace to pinpoint the error's location and offers a concrete input that triggers it. To facilitate error correction, we have also developed an interactive IDE that supports this process. We evaluated the effectiveness of this environment using the open-source database of C programs, CRATE, and a collection of real-world programs from the Linux kernel. The results demonstrate that the environment successfully identified 90% of the errors in CRATE and 75% of those in the Linux kernel suite. Furthermore, we observed that the automated workflow required minimal human intervention to locate and fix most errors. To support the adoption of this environment, we have made it publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenghuaiWu/TESTE.
